# Mexico Getting Started



[Mexico](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Genealogy "Mexico Genealogy")

[Research Tips and Strategies](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Research_Tips_and_Strategies "Mexico Research Tips and Strategies")

Getting Started

## Step 1: Gather and Choose

Before you begin, you should gather the following about the ancestor you are researching:

* First and last name
* Approximate date of a life event that happened in Mexico
* Specific town of residence in Mexico
  * *Note: If the place name you have is for a large city, be sure to review any family documents that mention where they came from. It is very possible that your ancestors came from somewhere near the city, but not the city itself. Finding any other place names in the records will help you narrow your search.*
* Name of a relative who also lived in Mexico (if possible)

Once you know the details above, choose a specific research goal, such as: "I want to find the marriage record for my great-grandparents" or "I want to locate the birth record for my great-aunt". This will help narrow your research and make it more effective.

Do you know the details necessary (shown above) to find the ancestor in Mexico?

* Yes — proceed to [Step 2: Find the Place](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Getting_Started#Step_2:_Find_the_Place "Mexico Getting Started").
* No — you should talk to any relatives who might know more and review any documents for additional clues. If needed, you can adjust your goal to search for an ancestor who you might have more clues for (the original person's child or spouse, for example).
  * If your ancestor was an immigrant to Mexico, see [Mexico Emigration and Immigration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Emigration_and_Immigration "Mexico Emigration and Immigration").
  * If your ancestor immigrated to the United States, see [Finding Town of Origin - United States Immigration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/GuidedResearch:Finding_Town_of_Origin_-_United_States_Immigration "GuidedResearch:Finding Town of Origin - United States Immigration") for additional guidance.

## Step 2: Find the Place

When you search for an ancestor in Mexico, it is important to know the specific town they lived in. This can help you to identify where the local civil registration office would have been, as well as where the local church was. Use online searches to learn more about where your ancestor lived (searches in Spanish usually yield more results).

* See [Mexico Gazetteers](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Gazetteers "Mexico Gazetteers") for more information.

If you can identify the town, proceed to [Step 3: Find the Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Getting_Started#Step_3:_Find_the_Records "Mexico Getting Started"). If you cannot identify the town, consider conducting more general online searches or reviewing other family records for additional details.

## Step 3: Find the Records

Certain record types will be more helpful than others when searching for ancestors in Mexico. These resources are most likely to help you learn more about your family:

### Religious Records

In Mexico, Catholicism has been the primary religion for centuries. Church records of baptism, marriage, and burial events can contain essential details about an ancestor’s life.

* See [Mexico Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Church_Records "Mexico Church Records") for more information.
* See the [FamilySearch Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/) for additional browsable images.

### Civil Registration (after 1859)

Civil registration was officially instituted by the local government in 1859, and by 1867 most areas were keeping records. While events that happened before civil registration began are not recorded here, births, marriages, and deaths that occurred after about 1867 were likely included in civil registration records.

* See [Mexico Civil Registration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration "Mexico Civil Registration") for more information.
* See the [FamilySearch Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/) for additional browsable images.

### Census Records (1930)

Several censuses have been taken throughout the history of Mexico. The 1930 census is available to search online.

* **1930** [Mexico Census, 1930](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1307314) at FamilySearch — [How to Use this Collection](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_National_Census,_1930_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records "Mexico National Census, 1930 - FamilySearch Historical Records"); index & images; *Also at: [Ancestry](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1771) ($)*

If you find a record, proceed to [Step 4: Evaluate](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Getting_Started#Step_4:_Evaluate "Mexico Getting Started"). If no applicable records are found, review your notes for date or place name discrepancies. You can also conduct online searches to learn more about archives you could contact to request more information.

## Step 4: Evaluate

Once you find a record for an ancestor, evaluate both the content of the record as well as if the record truly matches the ancestor you seek. Always study the original record if possible. The original records contain more details than was included in the database, and the index may contain errors.

After you have studied the record, determine your next steps. Identify the questions you still have about the person or their family, and consider which records are available for that place and time. Set goals for what you want to look for next, using clues from documents you already have to guide you toward any missing information.

## Step 5: Share

Before you finish, save everything you have found.

* Save links and write good notes in your sources so it is easy to relocate records as needed.
* Make sure you have recorded your new research goals so you know where to start next time.
* If you add the names of people or places to an online family tree, the best practice is to give the person their name at birth for their profile. If the person's name changed later in their life or they used a nickname, you can add other options as alternate names.

*Note: Keep in mind that some images of records may not be downloadable due to copyright and other restrictions. Be sure to capture image numbers or any other helpful information in your notes to help you find the record again later.*

Due to changes in contracts with record custodians, the availability of some FamilySearch record collections may change over time.

This website requires a paid subscription for full access. Some subscription websites are available for free at your local [FamilySearch Center or Affiliate Library](https://www.familysearch.org/centers/locations/).
